blocks.md: **The Lucas critique attacked 1960s macro models from theory; Sims (1980) attacked them from econometrics. Large models decided which variables were exogenous and which entered each equation by intuition, not theory — and once expectations matter, almost any variable could belong in any equation. His answer was the vector autoregression (VAR): treat every variable as endogenous and let each depend on the lags of all the others. Getting there takes time-series basics: macro data are autocorrelated, often non-stationary (differencing usually fixes that), and can be modelled as autoregressions whose lag length is chosen by ACF plots or information criteria. A VAR's coefficients are hard to read directly, so it is read through impulse responses, variance decompositions and Granger causality — none of which escapes the Lucas critique. Part 2 asks how to pull genuine economic shocks out of a VAR — recursive (Cholesky) orderings, narrative records, high-frequency market data, long-run restrictions — and, following Ramey's survey, what they say about monetary, fiscal and technology shocks.**

blocks.title: Sources and notation
blocks.md: This summary follows the slides of Chris Surro's lecture, covering both parts of "Working with Macroeconomic Data": sections 1–7 are Part 1, sections 8–14 Part 2, which follows Valerie Ramey's 2016 *Handbook of Macroeconomics* chapter. The coding assignment replicates Stock and Watson's three-variable VAR. $x_t$ is a time series at time $t$; $\Delta x_t = x_t - x_{t-1}$ is its first difference. The time-series theory is covered more technically in Econ 430.

sections.heading: 1. A different critique of 1950s and 60s macro

blocks.md: Last time: the Lucas critique — when policy changes, behavior changes, so models must account for it; the answers were microfoundations, rational expectations and DSGE models ([Econ 402A L8 Modern Macro Theory](note:econ-402a-l8-modern-macro-theory), [Lucas Critique](note:lucas-critique)). Today: a different critique, from econometrics.

**Review.** In a linear regression $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \varepsilon_i$, the left-hand variable $y$ is **endogenous** — explained by the model — and the right-hand $x_1, x_2$ are **exogenous**: inputs, not explained by the model, and assumed independent of the error ([Endogenous and Exogenous Variables](note:endogenous-and-exogenous-variables)).

Sims argued that econometric macro models were badly identified: "any variable which appears on the right-hand-side of one of these equations belongs in principle on the right-hand-side of all of them." Models ended up with different variables in different equations not by economic theory but by "an intuitive, econometrician's version of psychological and sociological theory".
His example was the FRB-MIT model, which explains consumption with one selection of variables and labor supply with an entirely different one.

It seems implausible that what affects consumption has no effect on labor supply. Expectations make it worse: U.S. consumers' tastes are unaffected by the temperature in Brazil, but reading of a frost in Brazil they might stockpile coffee in anticipation of its effect on price. So variables known to affect supply enter the demand equation, and vice versa, through expectations — undermining the exclusion restrictions econometricians had thought most reliable.

One solution is the DSGE approach of last lecture: define the structure of the economy explicitly. But Sims argued that choosing among policy regimes can often be done with reduced-form models of how policy affects the economy's evolution. His solution avoids any *a priori* judgement about which variables are exogenous: **all variables are endogenous**, and every variable can influence every other over time. That model is the **vector autoregression** ([Vector Autoregression](note:vector-autoregression)).
Paper summary: [Sims 1980 - Macroeconomics and Reality](note:sims-1980-macroeconomics-and-reality)

With cross-sectional data, $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$ can be estimated by OLS as long as the observations are independent and identically distributed — for example, cross-country regressions within a single year. With time series, $y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \varepsilon_t$, observations are rarely independent: if this month's inflation is high, next month's probably is too. The variable is **autocorrelated** (serially correlated).

**Stationarity.** A time series is stationary when its distribution does not depend on time: constant mean and variance, and no trend. Most time-series analysis needs stationary data, and the price level is clearly not stationary. A non-stationary series can often be made stationary by taking the **first difference**, $\Delta X_t = X_t - X_{t-1}$: the first difference of the (log) price level is inflation ([Stationarity and Unit Roots](note:stationarity-and-unit-roots)).

blocks.alt: US inflation, first difference of the price level

blocks.prompt: The US price level trends up throughout 1960–2025. What is the standard way to get a stationary series from it before estimating a VAR?

options.md: Take the first difference, $\Delta X_t = X_t - X_{t-1}$ (inflation)
Use more lags of the price level
options.feedback: Extra lags do not remove a trend; the series still has no constant mean.

options.md: Drop the years with the fastest price increases
options.feedback: That throws away data without removing the trend.

options.md: Estimate the model with OLS anyway; OLS does not need stationarity
options.feedback: The classical VAR assumptions require stationary data.

blocks.why: Differencing turns a trending level into its period-to-period change, which fluctuates around a mean. If one difference is not enough, difference again (the lecture's recipe allows first or second differences).

blocks.md: When a variable is serially correlated, it can be represented as a function of its own lags ([Autoregressive Model](note:autoregressive-model)). An AR(1) uses one lag,
and an AR($p$) uses $p$: $x_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{t-1} + \dots + \beta_p x_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t$. The coefficients are estimated by OLS.

blocks.caption: Inflation against its own lag: points lie close to a line with slope near one — strong persistence.

blocks.md: In an AR(1), $\beta_1$ is the share of a shock that carries into the next period, so a shock $\varepsilon$ is still worth $\beta_1^k\varepsilon$ after $k$ periods.

blocks.prompt: A shock of 2 hits a series with persistence 0.75: predict what is left four periods later

predict.ask: An AR(1) series with $\beta_1 = 0.75$ sits at its mean of 2 until a one-time shock of 2 hits in period 5. How much of the shock is left four periods later, in period 9?

blocks.md: The gap from the mean falls to $2(0.75) = 1.5$, then 1.125, 0.844 and $2(0.75)^4 = 0.633$; after 10 periods only 5.6% of the shock is left. Unlock $\beta_1$ to see faster decay at 0.5 and slower at 0.9.

**Testing for stationarity.** The **augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF)** test checks whether a series has a **unit root**: in $x_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, a unit root is $\beta_1 = 1$, so today's value is last period's plus noise. The Dickey-Fuller test's null hypothesis is $\beta_1 = 1$; the augmented version adds more lagged terms.

blocks.prompt: Set persistence to one: predict what happens to the shock

predict.ask: Now $\beta_1 = 1$, a unit root. A one-time shock of 2 hits in period 5. What does the series do afterwards?
options: It returns to 2, more slowly than with $\beta_1 = 0.75$
It stays at 4 for ever: the shock is permanent
It keeps rising by 2 every period
predict.why: With $\beta_1 = 1$ and no intercept, $x_t = x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$: a random walk. The shock moves the level to 4 and nothing brings it back, so the series has no mean to return to — it is not stationary. This is the null hypothesis of the ADF test.
feedback: With $\beta_1 = 1$ each period carries over all of the previous gap: nothing pulls it back.
That would need the shock to repeat (or a drift term). A one-time shock shifts the level once.

blocks.md: The **KPSS** (Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin) test is often paired with it, as a "reverse" ADF: its null hypothesis is that the series **is** stationary, so for stationarity you want to fail to reject.

blocks.prompt: For a stationary series, what should the ADF and KPSS tests show?

options.md: ADF rejects its null (a unit root); KPSS fails to reject its null (stationarity)
ADF fails to reject; KPSS rejects
options.feedback: That is the pattern for a series with a unit root.

options.md: Both reject their nulls
options.feedback: Rejecting KPSS's null is evidence *against* stationarity — the two tests would then disagree.

options.md: Both fail to reject their nulls
options.feedback: Then the data cannot tell a unit root from stationarity: the tests are inconclusive.

blocks.why: The two tests have opposite nulls. ADF's null is non-stationarity, so rejecting it supports stationarity; KPSS's null is stationarity, so failing to reject it is consistent with it. Running both guards against a test that simply has low power.

blocks.md: Classical VAR assumptions require stationary data; in certain applications that can be relaxed (next time).

To estimate an AR model, and later a VAR, you must decide how many lags to include, using ACF plots or an information criterion. An **information criterion** balances how well a model fits against the risk of overfitting ([Model Selection Criteria](note:model-selection-criteria)):
where $k$ is the number of lags (more precisely, of estimated parameters), $L$ the maximized likelihood and $n$ the number of observations. Choose the model with the **minimum** value.

blocks.prompt: With $n = 100$ observations, an AR model with 2 lags has $\ln L = -100$ and one with 4 lags has $\ln L = -98.5$. Using $k$ as the number of lags, which model do AIC and BIC choose?

options.md: Both choose 2 lags
Both choose 4 lags, because it fits better
options.feedback: It fits better ($\ln L$ is higher), but not by enough to pay for two more parameters.

options.md: AIC chooses 4 lags and BIC chooses 2
options.feedback: AIC is 204 with 2 lags and 205 with 4: AIC also prefers 2.

options.md: AIC chooses 2 lags and BIC chooses 4
options.feedback: BIC penalizes parameters more ($\ln 100 = 4.6$ per parameter against AIC's 2), so it never prefers the bigger model when AIC doesn't.

blocks.why: AIC: $2(2) + 200 = 204$ against $2(4) + 197 = 205$. BIC: $2\ln 100 + 200 = 209.2$ against $4\ln 100 + 197 = 215.4$. Both pick the smaller model.

blocks.md: An **autocorrelation function (ACF)** plot shows the correlation of a variable with each of its lags. A **partial autocorrelation function (PACF)** plot isolates the direct effect of each lag: $x_{t-4}$ affects $x_t$ directly and also indirectly through $x_{t-1}$, $x_{t-2}$ and $x_{t-3}$, and the PACF removes the indirect part.

blocks.caption: ACF of inflation: correlations decay slowly and stay well above the significance band for many lags — the signature of a highly persistent, possibly non-stationary series.
ACF of differenced inflation: only the first couple of lags are clearly positive, with smaller swings after.

blocks.md: An AR model can then forecast the future path of a variable.

blocks.caption: An AR forecast (orange) of US inflation.

blocks.md: An AR model makes a variable a function of its own lags. A **vector autoregression** makes each variable a function of its own lags **and the lags of every other variable** in the model, so every variable is endogenous. A two-variable VAR with one lag:
The number of parameters grows quickly with variables and lags: with $k$ variables and $p$ lags, each of the $k$ equations has $kp$ lag coefficients and an intercept.

blocks.prompt: How many parameters must be estimated in a VAR with $k = 6$ variables and 5 lags?

wrongCompute.md: each of the $k$ equations also has an intercept
each equation includes 5 lags of *every* variable, not just its own

blocks.why: $k^2p + k = 36 \times 5 + 6 = 186$ — the lecture's example. This is why standard VARs use only a few variables: each one added costs many degrees of freedom.

blocks.md: Assuming stationary data, the parameters are estimated equation by equation with OLS. But interpreting the coefficients is tricky. In $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + \varepsilon_i$, $\beta_1$ is the average change in $y$ when $x_1$ rises one unit holding everything else constant; in a VAR every variable is endogenous, so you cannot hold the others constant, and isolating one variable's impact on another is hard. Three tools help.

**Impulse response functions (IRFs).** Shock the error of one equation once, and trace the path of every variable over time using the estimated coefficients — the AR impulse response above, for a whole system.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Stock and Watson 2001 - impulse responses in the inflation-unemployment-interest rate VAR.png
blocks.alt: Stock and Watson 2001 - impulse responses in the inflation-unemployment-interest rate VAR
blocks.caption: Stock and Watson's three-variable VAR: each panel traces one variable's response to a one-time shock to one equation, with confidence bands.

blocks.md: Paper summary: [Stock and Watson 2001 - Vector Autoregressions](note:stock-and-watson-2001-vector-autoregressions)

**Forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD).** How much of the variance of each variable is explained by its own shocks versus shocks to the other variables: is inflation's path mainly driven by past inflation shocks, or by shocks to other variables?

**Granger causality.** A statistical version of causality: do past values of $X$ help predict current values of $Y$ beyond what past values of $Y$ alone predict? It does not necessarily imply true causality.

blocks.prompt: A central bank raises interest rates whenever inflation is high, and higher rates lower inflation. What would a VAR of inflation and the interest rate most likely show?

options.md: Inflation Granger-causes the interest rate, even though the policy causes inflation to fall
The interest rate Granger-causes inflation, and inflation does not Granger-cause the interest rate
options.feedback: Rates respond to past inflation, so past inflation does help predict rates.

options.md: Neither Granger-causes the other, because the effects cancel
options.feedback: Each variable's past helps predict the other; Granger causality measures prediction, not net effects.

options.md: Granger causality would reveal that rates truly cause inflation
options.feedback: Granger causality is about prediction; it cannot settle true causation without a structural model.

blocks.why: Past inflation predicts future rate rises, so in the data inflation "Granger-causes" interest rates — even though the causal story of interest is the reverse. To identify true causality you need a structural model.

blocks.md: **Recap — estimating a VAR:**

1. Test the data for stationarity (ADF and KPSS).
2. If not stationary, transform the data (first or second differences).
3. Choose the number of lags (ACF/PACF plots or information criteria).
4. Estimate the model; plot impulse responses, test Granger causality, compute the FEVD.

sections.heading: 7. Do VARs solve the Lucas critique?

blocks.md: Not really. VARs still estimate relationships from past data, and those relationships are almost certainly not independent of the policy environment. DSGE models are still needed to model the underlying mechanisms explicitly.

The VARs above are **reduced-form**. A **structural VAR** (SVAR) uses theory to impose specific restrictions on the parameters, usually so that the shocks are uncorrelated, which makes it easier to isolate the effect of a specific shock. Part 2 is about exactly that: how macroeconomists over the past 30 years have identified shocks with VARs.

sections.heading: 8. Part 2: levels or differences, and the coding assignment

blocks.md: Part 2 explains the coding assignment and then follows Valerie Ramey's 2016 *Handbook of Macroeconomics* chapter through examples of VARs in macroeconomic research.

**Is stationarity necessary?** Strictly, a VAR's standard theory needs stationary data. But Sims, Stock and Watson (1990) show that for most results, estimating the VAR in **levels** still gives consistent estimates, while taking first differences throws away important information about the long-run relationships between variables. They recommend estimating most macro VARs in **log levels** rather than first differences — with care when doing inference (hypothesis tests) on non-stationary data ([Stationarity and Unit Roots](note:stationarity-and-unit-roots)).

blocks.prompt: Part 1's recipe says to difference non-stationary series before estimating a VAR. What do Sims, Stock and Watson (1990) recommend for most macro VARs instead?

options.md: Estimate in log levels: the estimates stay consistent, and differencing throws away information on long-run relationships
Always take second differences to be safe
options.feedback: Over-differencing discards even more information about how the variables move together.

options.md: Detrend every series with the HP filter first
options.feedback: That is a business-cycle filtering choice, not their recommendation for VARs.

options.md: Drop the non-stationary variables from the VAR
options.feedback: Prices and output are non-stationary and are exactly what macro VARs study.

blocks.why: Consistency survives in levels for most results, and the levels keep the information that differencing removes. The cost is inference: hypothesis tests on non-stationary data need care.

blocks.md: **The coding assignment** replicates [Stock and Watson 2001 - Vector Autoregressions](note:stock-and-watson-2001-vector-autoregressions): a three-variable VAR in inflation, the unemployment rate and the federal funds rate to measure the effects of monetary policy, with impulse responses, Granger causality and a variance decomposition. The tasks: (1) download the data, (2) replicate Stock and Watson's basic results in Python, (3) update with more recent data, (4) test on another country, (5) make good visualizations, (6) put it together in one PDF. Paper summary: [Ramey 2016 - Macroeconomic Shocks and Their Propagation](note:ramey-2016-macroeconomic-shocks-and-their-propagation)

Ramey examines how three kinds of shocks affect the economy — **monetary, fiscal and technology** — mainly through VARs. In her framework an economic shock must satisfy three properties ([Structural Shock Identification](note:structural-shock-identification)):
Identifying such shocks is very difficult, and is the main challenge in this literature.

blocks.prompt: The government announces in January a spending increase that takes effect in July. Why is the July rise in spending a poor "shock" for estimating its effects?

options.md: It was anticipated: people and firms could react from January, so July is not a surprise
It is correlated with tax shocks
options.feedback: Nothing in the story ties it to taxes; the problem is timing.

options.md: Government spending is never exogenous
options.feedback: Military build-ups driven by wars are often treated as exogenous; this one fails a different test.

options.md: Spending only affects output with a lag
options.feedback: Lags are fine for an impulse response; what matters is whether the shock was a surprise.

blocks.why: A shock must be unanticipated as well as exogenous and uncorrelated. With six months' warning, behavior changes before the spending arrives, so a VAR that dates the shock in July mis-times its effects — Ramey's "foresight by agents".

blocks.md: Estimate a VAR in inflation, unemployment and the interest rate by OLS:

where $\eta$ is the OLS residual. If these residuals ("innovations") were uncorrelated, there would be no identification problem: we could separate inflation, unemployment and interest-rate shocks. Usually we can't assume that. Suppose instead the innovations are related within the period:

where the $\varepsilon$ terms are the **structural shocks** — actual economic shocks such as the outbreak of a war or an unexpected policy change. As written, this system is unidentified: we have data on 3 objects but need to estimate 6 parameters, so we need **3 more restrictions**.

blocks.prompt: A VAR has $k = 3$ variables. How many restrictions on the within-period relationships between the innovations does a recursive (Cholesky) ordering impose?

wrongCompute.md: that is the number of within-period coefficients $b_{ij}$; the ordering sets half of them to zero
the diagonal is not a parameter: each innovation is not regressed on itself

blocks.why: There are $k(k - 1)$ off-diagonal coefficients $b_{ij}$, and the covariances of the innovations pin down only half of them, so $k(k-1)/2$ must be restricted — for $k = 3$, three zeros ($b_{31} = b_{32} = b_{21} = 0$). A recursive ordering does exactly that: everything above (or below) the diagonal is zero.

blocks.md: **Recursive ordering.** One solution: assume certain shocks are unrelated to certain variables and order the equations recursively. For example, assume the interest rate is unaffected within the period by shocks to inflation or unemployment ($b_{31} = b_{32} = 0$), and unemployment unaffected by shocks to inflation ($b_{21} = 0$). The system becomes
and the remaining parameters can be estimated with OLS. This is the **Cholesky decomposition**, or "triangularization".

Once the structural shocks are identified, impulse responses follow in three steps: (1) set one structural shock equal to 1; (2) calculate the VAR innovations that shock implies, using the estimated relationships; (3) feed those innovations through the original reduced-form VAR to trace the path of each variable.

blocks.prompt: In the recursive system above, suppose $b_{23} = 0.5$, $b_{12} = 0.4$ and $b_{13} = 0.1$. An interest-rate shock sets $\varepsilon_{3t} = 1$ (and the other structural shocks are 0). What is the inflation innovation $\eta_{1t}$?

wrong.md: that is only the direct effect $b_{13}\eta_{3t}$; the shock also moves unemployment, which moves inflation
that is only the effect through unemployment, $b_{12}\eta_{2t}$; add the direct effect

blocks.why: Work down the ordering: $\eta_{3t} = 1$, then $\eta_{2t} = 0.5 \times 1 = 0.5$, then $\eta_{1t} = 0.4 \times 0.5 + 0.1 \times 1 = 0.3$. These innovations are step 2; feeding them through the reduced-form VAR gives the impulse response.

blocks.md: **Other identification methods:**

- **Narrative approach:** estimate structural shocks directly from historical information — usually still combined with a recursive ordering.
- **High-frequency data:** more likely to isolate exogenous shocks (market moves in minutes around an announcement).
- **Instrumental variables:** estimate the structural shocks indirectly through external instruments ([Instrumental Variables and 2SLS](note:instrumental-variables-and-2sls)).
- **Other restrictions:** long-run restrictions, sign restrictions, restrictions from a DSGE model.

**The problem of foresight.** Ramey notes two more problems. **Foresight by agents:** if shocks are anticipated, even a properly identified structural shock may not give clean estimates — an anticipated policy change does not affect the economy the way an unanticipated one does. **Foresight by policymakers:** policymakers often have more information than the model includes, so the model may be capturing the policymaker responding to changing expectations about the future that are missing from the model.

Early VARs suggested a relatively small role for monetary policy, and RBC models of the same period reached similar conclusions ([Real Business Cycle Model](note:real-business-cycle-model)). Pushback came from Romer and Romer (1989), who identified monetary shocks with a narrative approach, and Bernanke and Blinder (1992), who used interest-rate shocks instead of money-supply shocks. Both found larger effects.

**The price puzzle.** Early VARs tended to find that prices *rose* after a monetary tightening — the opposite of what theory suggests. Sims (1992): the Fed uses much more information than a typical VAR includes. Including commodity prices (often gold or oil) can proxy expectations about future inflation; another option is to include many more variables with a factor-augmented VAR (FAVAR).

blocks.prompt: Why might a small VAR show prices rising after the Fed raises interest rates?

options.md: The Fed raises rates when it expects inflation, using information the VAR leaves out, so the "shock" partly reflects coming inflation
Higher interest rates raise firms' costs, so prices rise permanently
options.feedback: That cost channel is possible but would not explain why the puzzle disappears once commodity prices are added.

options.md: Prices are sticky, so they cannot respond to policy
options.feedback: Sticky prices respond slowly, not in the wrong direction.

options.md: The VAR was estimated in levels instead of differences
options.feedback: Estimating in levels is usually fine for consistency; the puzzle is about missing information.

blocks.why: This is foresight by the policymaker: the identified shock is not exogenous to future inflation. Adding commodity prices (a proxy for expected inflation) or many more variables (FAVAR) gives the VAR the Fed's information, and the puzzle largely goes away.

**Example 3: Gertler and Karadi (2015).** Add financial variables to the monetary VAR and incorporate forward guidance. Traditional identification is then hard to justify — financial-market variables almost certainly respond immediately to policy shocks. The solution: use shocks to Fed funds futures as a high-frequency indicator (HFI). The results are relatively similar.

**Identifying fiscal shocks.** Many papers treat **military spending** as plausibly exogenous — driven by wars, not by the macroeconomy — sometimes combined with a narrative approach. The **recursive approach**, as for monetary policy, assumes spending or tax shocks only affect spending or taxes within the period; it tends to find smaller effects and is more exposed to foresight problems.

**Estimating multipliers.** Many papers use VARs to estimate the size of the spending or tax multiplier ([Keynesian Multiplier](note:keynesian-multiplier)). Estimates range from **0.6 to 1.5 for spending** and **−0.5 to −5 for taxes**. Disagreement remains on what to measure: the ratio of the **peak** responses of output and government spending, or of their **integrals** (cumulative responses).

blocks.prompt: Illustrative numbers: after a spending shock, government spending is 1, 1 and 0.5 above normal in quarters 0–2, and output is 0.6, 0.9 and 0.6 above normal. What is the cumulative (integral) multiplier over the three quarters? Give two decimals.

wrong.md: that is the peak multiplier, peak output response over peak spending response
that is the impact multiplier in quarter 0
that divides cumulative spending by cumulative output; the multiplier is output over spending

blocks.why: Cumulative output $0.6 + 0.9 + 0.6 = 2.1$ over cumulative spending $1 + 1 + 0.5 = 2.5$ gives 0.84; the peak ratio is $0.9/1 = 0.9$. Same impulse responses, different multipliers — one reason published estimates disagree.

blocks.md: **Example: Blanchard and Perotti (2002).** Take the three-equation system above, but let the equations be the residuals of **taxes**, **government spending** and **GDP**. Blanchard and Perotti assume $b_{21} = b_{23} = 0$ — only government spending shocks have an immediate effect on spending — and take $b_{13} = 2.08$ from the literature. *(In the system as written, $b_{13}$ is how much the tax innovation responds within the quarter to the GDP innovation: tax revenue moving automatically with output.)*

Technology (TFP) shocks are usually estimated with DSGE models; early models used the Solow residual ([Solow Residual](note:solow-residual)). Problems: money, interest rates and government spending **Granger-cause** the Solow residual (Evans 1992) — technology should not respond to them; and after adjusting the residual for factors such as the utilization of labor and capital, its strong effects disappear. Technology shocks as estimated might not cause business-cycle movements at all.

**Galí (1999)** uses the RBC model's own assumption — in the long run only productivity shocks affect productivity — to identify a VAR: first a bivariate VAR in productivity and hours, then a five-variable model adding real balances, interest rates and inflation. He finds that technology shocks do not produce the majority of business-cycle fluctuations, as an RBC model would predict. Later papers have used different assumptions to try to restore the classic RBC results.

blocks.prompt: In Galí's VAR, a positive technology shock raises productivity but lowers hours on impact, and the technology components of output and hours are negatively correlated. What does this imply for the RBC model?

options.md: Technology shocks cannot be the main source of business cycles, in which output and hours rise and fall together
It confirms the RBC model: technology shocks move hours
options.feedback: The RBC model predicts hours *rise* with a positive technology shock; here they fall.

options.md: The long-run restriction must be wrong, because the RBC model is right
options.feedback: That is one possible response (later papers try other assumptions), but it is not what the estimates imply.

options.md: Technology shocks have no effect on output
options.feedback: GDP rises after the shock; what fails is the co-movement with hours.

blocks.why: Business cycles are periods when output and hours move together. If technology shocks push them in opposite directions, the co-movement must come from other (non-technology) shocks — the opposite of the RBC claim. When theory and evidence conflict, one can still ask whether the model or the identification is wrong.

blocks.md: Paper summary: [Gali 1999 - Technology, Employment, and the Business Cycle](note:gali-1999-technology-employment-and-the-business-cycle)

**News shocks.** Beaudry and Portier (2006) use stock market data as a proxy for expectations about future productivity and find a large role for news shocks. Problems: the model may not be properly identified, and future TFP changes may not show up in stock prices at all — big innovations tend to happen in private companies before they go public.

sections.heading: 14. Other shocks, combining them, and where we stand

blocks.md: Other shocks used less often in VARs: **oil** shocks, **credit** shocks, **policy uncertainty**, and **labor market** shocks.

Ramey combines what she considers the most promising shock series into one VAR and asks how much of the forecast-error variance of output and hours each explains ([US Sources of Output and Hours Fluctuations 1954-2005](note:us-sources-of-output-and-hours-fluctuations-1954-2005)).

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Ramey 2016 combined VAR forecast error variance decomposition.png
blocks.alt: Table - Ramey 2016 combined VAR forecast error variance decomposition

blocks.md: Together the identified shocks explain about 78% of output's forecast-error variance on impact and 63% at five years. News about investment-specific technology and shocks to the marginal efficiency of investment matter most; monetary policy (the federal funds rate) explains 7–8% of output at two to five years and up to 18% of hours; each fiscal shock explains under 10% of output.

**Where do we stand?** Ramey concludes that we are making progress on which shocks drive the economy, but there is still a long way to go. When the empirical evidence and theory conflict, do we assume the theory is wrong or the empirical model is mis-specified?

sections.heading: What to be able to do

blocks.md:
1. Explain Sims's critique of large-scale macro models and why a VAR treats every variable as endogenous.
2. Define stationarity, explain why differencing helps and when estimating in levels is preferred, and read ACF plots.
3. Write and interpret an AR($p$) model, including the decay of a shock in an AR(1) and what a unit root means.
4. State the null hypotheses of the ADF and KPSS tests and use AIC and BIC to choose lags.
5. Write a VAR and count its parameters.
6. Interpret impulse responses, variance decompositions and Granger causality, and explain why VARs do not escape the Lucas critique.

7. State what makes a structural shock, count the restrictions needed, and identify shocks with a recursive (Cholesky) ordering to start an impulse response.
8. Describe narrative, high-frequency, instrumental-variable and long-run identification, and the foresight problems (including the price puzzle).
9. Summarize the evidence on monetary, fiscal and technology shocks: larger monetary effects with better identification, multipliers measured as peaks or integrals, and Galí's challenge to the RBC model.
